original_summary: Helen Keller has learned to copy finger-spelled words, but she does not yet understand that they have meaning. After becoming frustrated and breaking her doll, she goes with her teacher to a well-house. When her teacher spells “water” into one hand while cold water flows over the other, Helen suddenly understands that words name things. On the way home, she learns several more words and later feels sorry when she sees the broken doll.
seed_elements: Helen, who is deaf and blind, is frustrated because finger-spelling still seems like a meaningless game.
She breaks her new rag doll in anger and feels no remorse at first.
Her teacher takes her to the outdoor pump or well-house.
Cold running water flows over one hand while the teacher spells “w-a-t-e-r” into the other.
Helen suddenly understands that the hand movements are a name for the water and that things have names.
She learns more words on the way back, then sees the broken doll, feels sorry, and tries to repair it.
discarded_elements: Detailed events from the surrounding weeks of lessons
Later events from Helen’s life and autobiography
Extra historical background and technical detail about finger-spelling
Minor descriptions and additional people not needed for the scene
conversion_plan: Keep the historical setting, including the well-house, water pump, and rag doll, because these details are central to the real event. Tell the story in the first person as Helen, using simple A2-level language and about 300–350 words. Preserve the full sequence from frustration and breaking the doll to the discovery that “water” has meaning, followed by learning more words and feeling remorse.
